notes.b: A natural resource is a material or energy source taken from the environment, such as fuels, water, minerals, timber, wind and sunlight. Because some resources run out and others do not, what we use and how we use it matters for the future.
points: Sustainable use means meeting present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs, so resources are still there for the people who come after us.
Resources are classed by how quickly they are replaced: renewable resources are replenished naturally, while non-renewable resources are finite (limited in supply).
Consumers influence resource use through what they buy, how long they keep products in use and how they dispose of them, so everyday choices add up.

Consumers conserve resources by buying only what is needed, choosing durable and repairable goods, and using items fully before replacing them, which means fewer new materials and less energy are used.
notes.tip: Do not treat 'sustainable' and 'renewable' as the same word: a renewable source used faster than it is replaced, such as an over-felled forest, is not sustainable. If asked to list consumer responsibilities, think of reducing pollution, choosing renewable resources, thinking about disposal and recycling to save landfill space.

notes.b: A renewable resource is naturally replenished and is not used up by constant use, provided it is used no faster than it is replaced. Each renewable energy source works by turning a natural movement or heat into electricity or heat for buildings.
points: Solar energy: photovoltaic (PV) panels convert sunlight directly into electricity, and solar thermal panels use sunlight to heat water. Passive solar design, which sites the house and its glazing towards the sun, uses sunlight for heat and light.

Wind energy: turbines convert the kinetic energy (movement energy) of moving air into electricity; wind farms are usually sited on exposed upland and coastal land, or at sea, where the wind is strongest.

Hydroelectric energy: falling or flowing water turns turbines, so the source depends on a steady flow of water and a difference in height. The Shannon Scheme at Ardnacrusha, opened in 1929, is an Irish example.
Biomass: wood, straw, energy crops and plant or animal waste are burned, or converted to biogas, to release heat or electricity.
Geothermal energy: heat stored in the earth's crust is brought to the surface as hot water or steam to heat buildings or generate electricity.
Tidal energy uses the rise and fall of the tides to drive turbines; wave energy uses the motion of waves to drive devices.

Renewable heat in the home comes from heat pumps (which take low-grade heat from the air, ground or water), solar thermal panels, and stoves burning wood from managed forests. Heat pumps count as renewable heat because most of their heat comes from air, ground or water.
Hydrogen can also carry energy, but it is renewable only if it is made using renewable electricity.
notes.tip: When asked to name renewable sources, choose from solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass, tidal and wave. Biomass is renewable only if the plants are regrown, and burning it still releases carbon dioxide (carbon the plants recently took from the air), so never say it gives no emissions.

notes.h: Benefits and limits of renewable energy
notes.b: Renewable energy is attractive because it does not run out and is cleaner to produce, but it is not free of drawbacks. Exam answers need both sides.
points: Renewable sources are sustainable: their supply does not run out on human timescales, so a well sited and maintained system can last indefinitely.
Most produce little or no air pollution or carbon dioxide while generating energy, which reduces damage to air and water.
Using renewables reduces dependence on imported fuel, which improves energy security (a dependable supply that does not rely on other countries).
Some renewables can be installed in a home, such as solar panels on a roof or a small wind turbine, so energy is produced where it is used.
Building, maintaining and manufacturing renewable systems creates employment, and running costs are low once the system is installed.
Limitation: wind and solar output varies with weather and daylight, so storage or a backup supply is needed.
Limitation: installation costs can be high, and hydro and tidal systems need suitable sites.
Limitation: wind farms and dams can affect the landscape and habitats.
notes.tip: Renewable does not mean no disadvantages. When a question asks for advantages and disadvantages of a renewable source, give both, and for 'sustainability' say that it is replaced naturally so it can last.

notes.b: A non-renewable resource is limited in supply and cannot be replaced within a human lifetime once it is used up. Fuels and minerals dug out of the ground fall into this group.
points: Fossil fuels are coal, oil, natural gas and peat, formed from the remains of plants and animals over very long periods: peat over thousands of years, coal, oil and gas over millions. Coke and anthracite (a type of coal) are other fuels in this group.

Peat (turf) is cut from bogs for home heating and electricity generation. Bogs regrow far too slowly to count as renewable, so peat is a non-renewable fossil fuel, and bog habitats do not regenerate quickly.
Nuclear energy uses uranium, a mined, finite fuel, so it is non-renewable. Ireland has no nuclear power station.
Iron ore, copper ore and bauxite (the ore of aluminium) are non-renewable mineral resources because they are mined and finite; recycling extends the life of the metal they yield.
For one non-renewable source used in the home, give the source and an advantage: fossil fuels are concentrated, give a lot of heat, and have an established supply and appliances.
The disadvantages are that the fuel is finite, its price rises as reserves fall, burning it causes emissions and extracting it damages the land. For these reasons it is not sustainable.
notes.tip: Nuclear is non-renewable because uranium is finite, so never list it beside renewable examples. Peat is also non-renewable, even though bogs slowly regrow. For a discussion of one non-renewable source in the home, cover the source, an advantage, a disadvantage and why it is not sustainable.

notes.b: Using non-renewable resources harms the environment twice: when they are extracted and when they are burned. As they become scarce, the supply itself also becomes a problem.
points: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas (a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere), which contributes to global warming and climate change.
Burning coal, oil and peat releases sulphur dioxide, which forms acid rain.
Mining, quarrying, drilling and peat extraction destroy habitats and landscapes, so the wildlife that lived there loses its home.
Cutting bogs releases stored carbon, which adds to the carbon dioxide in the air.
As reserves fall, fuel becomes harder and more costly to extract, so supplies become less secure.
notes.tip: Remember the pairing: carbon dioxide causes global warming and sulphur dioxide causes acid rain.

notes.b: Consumers are responsible for how they use resources because their daily choices decide how much fuel is burned and how much material is thrown away. Practical steps cut demand for non-renewable resources and support renewable ones.
points: Reduce energy demand, for example by insulating the home, using appliances efficiently and switching off standby, so less fossil fuel is burned.
Choose a renewable electricity supplier, or install a renewable system such as solar panels or a heat pump, where practical. Smokeless or renewable fuel is also a better choice.
Buy wood and paper products certified by a recognised scheme such as FSC (Forest Stewardship Council) or PEFC, which confirms that the timber came from managed forests.
Reuse and recycle metals, glass and paper so that finite materials are used again.
Choose products made with recycled content, which means less new material has to be mined or felled.
notes.tip: For 'consumer responsibilities', link each action to its reason: reduce pollution, choose renewable resources, think about disposal, and recycle to save landfill space.

keyTerms.definition: A material or energy source taken from the natural environment for human use.
A resource that is naturally replenished and is not used up by constant use, provided it is used no faster than it is replaced.
A resource that is limited in supply and cannot be replaced on human timescales once it is used up.
A resource whose supply is fixed, so it will eventually be used up.
Using resources in a way that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
A fuel such as coal, oil, natural gas or peat, formed from the remains of organisms over very long periods.
Plant and animal material used as a fuel, either burned directly or converted to biogas.
Heat stored in the earth's crust, which is used for heating buildings or generating electricity.
A panel that converts sunlight directly into electricity.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide, that traps heat in the atmosphere.

factCards.definition: Solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass, tidal and wave energy.
Coal, oil, natural gas and peat.
They do not run out on human timescales; they produce little or no pollution during operation; they reduce dependence on imported fuel.
Output varies with weather and daylight, so storage or a backup supply is needed; installation costs can be high for systems such as solar panels and turbines.

factCards.term: Three effects of burning fossil fuels
factCards.definition: Carbon dioxide adds to global warming; sulphur dioxide forms acid rain; particulates and nitrogen oxides harm the respiratory health of people nearby.

factCards.term: Two ways to conserve energy at home
factCards.definition: Insulate the home to cut heating demand; use appliances efficiently so less electricity is needed.
Iron ore, copper ore and bauxite (aluminium ore).

questions.prompt: Identify two renewable energy sources and describe one environmental benefit of using renewable energy rather than fossil fuels.
questions.model: Two correctly named renewable sources, from solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass, tidal and wave energy. One benefit, fully explained: renewable sources produce little or no carbon dioxide or pollution while generating energy, so they reduce global warming and air pollution. Alternatively: they do not run out, so supply is sustainable and does not deplete the environment.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between renewable and non-renewable resources, giving two examples of each. Describe the environmental effects of using non-renewable energy, and outline how a household can reduce its dependence on it.
questions.model: Definition of a renewable resource as naturally replenished and not used up by constant use, with two named examples such as solar or wind energy. Definition of a non-renewable resource as limited in supply and not replaced once used up, with two named examples such as coal or peat. Environmental effects: carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels adds to global warming; sulphur dioxide forms acid rain; mining and peat extraction destroy habitats. Household measures: insulate the home and draught-proof it to reduce heating demand; use appliances efficiently and switch off standby; choose a renewable electricity supplier or install a renewable system such as solar panels; reuse and recycle materials to reduce demand for new resources.
